# Notes on 2 Corinthians 11, verse by verse

**What I was able to read.** I read the full text of Guzik's Enduring Word commentary (vv. 1–14; I only have a summary for the rest), the Pulpit Commentary (vv. 1–15 in full, plus excerpts for vv. 16–23) and Sam Storms's outline of the whole chapter. For everything else I only saw search excerpts: BibleHub (Ellicott, Barnes, Gill), StudyLight, Precept Austin, Wayne Barber, and Chrysostom on newadvent.org.

**What's missing.**
- **Protestant traditions:** I found no Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan or Anglican writer on this chapter apart from the Pulpit Commentary (an older British work). So I couldn't really cover point 2. The only real disagreement I found is over who the "super-apostles" were (v. 5).
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** I only have scattered remarks from Chrysostom.
- **Modern scholarship:** I didn't get to netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org.
- **Popular modern teaching:** No source I read discusses prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching directly.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik says Paul calls defending himself "folly" not because it is nonsense. He does it reluctantly, has better things to do, and knows some Corinthians will think his idea of honour is foolish. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-11/
- Pulpit says the "folly" is the foolishness of boasting, and "fool/folly" keep coming back through this section. It reads "bear with me" as a statement ("you really do bear with me"), a kind acknowledgement of their goodwill. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/11.htm
- Ellicott notes that "bearing with" occurs five times and "folly" or "fool" at least eight times in this section. He thinks Paul is echoing what his opponents said, something like "we can't put up with his folly any longer." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/11-1.htm
- Storms says Paul is being sarcastic, but the stakes aren't his reputation. The opponents offered a "different" Christianity that was really no gospel at all, so eternal destiny was at issue. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/2-corinthians-11:1-33

**v. 2**
- Guzik: human jealousy is a vice, but sharing God's jealousy for his people is a virtue. Paul is like the "friend of the bridegroom" who guards the bride during the betrothal. In that culture, unfaithfulness during betrothal counted as adultery. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-11/
- Pulpit: the word means both jealousy and zeal, and literally "a jealousy of God." The church was betrothed to Christ when it was converted, and Paul will present it as a pure bride when Christ returns. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/11.htm
- Storms sees three stages: betrothal (conversion), engagement (this present age) and wedding (Christ's return). The phrase could mean Paul is filled with "God's own zeal." https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/2-corinthians-11:1-33
- Chrysostom (Orthodox and Catholic Church Father) uses this verse when he describes marriage as a picture of Christ's union with the Church. He calls marriage "a mystery of the Church", since Christ united with her in a spiritual union. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230312.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik says Satan's lie to Eve came wrapped in half-truths. The Corinthians' temptation was "triumphalism," which was attractive because it was mixed with true teaching about victory in Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-11/
- Pulpit: Paul still treats their falling away as a fear for the future, not something already done. "Simplicity" means single-minded loyalty directed toward Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/11.htm
- MacArthur (via Precept Austin) says "I am afraid" sums up Paul's concern in the whole letter. His defence, his appeals and his confrontation of the false teachers were all driven by this fear. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-11-commentary
- Storms, citing Barnett: Eve stands for the Corinthian church and the serpent for the false apostles. Because the verse stresses the *mind*, what we believe about Jesus shapes our love for him. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/2-corinthians-11:1-33
- Chrysostom cites this verse to show that the apostles did not fear death, but they did fear that their disciples might be lost. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23102.htm

**v. 4** (readings genuinely differ)
- Guzik: since the Corinthians despised Paul's weakness, the "other Jesus" was probably a "super Jesus" who knew no suffering or death, and such a Jesus cannot save. The real problem was that the church put up with these teachers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-11/
- Pulpit reads it differently. The newcomer seemed to preach the *same* Jesus, so Paul is being ironic: they had even less excuse for preferring him over the one who first brought them Christ and the Spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/11.htm
- Ellicott says the singular "he that cometh" points to one individual teacher who had become prominent. Barnes considers a serious reading as well: if the false teacher could offer a better Saviour, it would make sense to receive him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/11-4.htm
- Storms, citing Barnett: Paul says "Jesus" rather than "Christ," which may point to a stress on Jesus' Jewish earthly life at the expense of his risen lordship. "Different spirit" most likely means tolerating teachers energised by demons, not demonic possession of believers. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/2-corinthians-11:1-33
- Barber says the "different spirit" was a spirit of bondage, fear and judgmentalism instead of the Holy Spirit. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-11-commentary-wayne-barber

**v. 5** (who were the "super-apostles"?)
- Guzik: commentators argue warmly about this. Peter or Apollos is unlikely; Paul is probably mocking the false apostles. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-11/
- Pulpit: the strange word shows strong feeling, roughly "extra-super" apostles. It says Paul is not criticising the Twelve. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/11.htm
- Gill (Baptist) allows a different reading. He names Peter, James and John as possible "very chiefest apostles", though he also offers the ironic reading. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/11-5.html
- Ellicott says it is "the insanity of controversy" to link this verse to the question of Peter's primacy. He sees the targets as false teachers, perhaps claiming to be delegates of the Jerusalem church. https://biblehub.com/2_corinthians/11-5.htm
- BibleHub surveys the scholarly options: Jewish-Christian intruders (Judaizers), travelling teachers influenced by philosophy, or charismatic leaders in the church who prized visions and revelations. https://biblehub.com/q/who_were_the_'super-apostles'.htm

**v. 6**
- Guzik: Paul wasn't polished by the standards of Greek rhetoric, but he was honest and open with them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-11/
- Pulpit: the word means a "layman" in speaking, without professional training. Paul did claim spiritual knowledge. Pulpit says the better manuscripts read "making it [my knowledge] known." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/11.htm
- Storms, citing Barnett: Paul being "inferior" to trained speakers doesn't mean he was a poor preacher. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/2-corinthians-11:1-33

**v. 7**
- Guzik: speakers who charged nothing were often seen as amateurs. Paul's "Did I sin?" is heavy irony. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-11/
- Pulpit: critics argued that if Paul really had authority he would have taken support. Tent-making was a despised trade. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/11.htm
- Storms: Paul was caught either way. Refusing pay looked like he knew he had no authority; accepting it looked like greed. Storms gives four reasons for Paul's policy, including integrity and freedom from pressure by wealthy members. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/2-corinthians-11:1-33

**v. 8**
- Guzik: "robbed" was used in classical Greek for stripping a dead soldier's armour. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-11/
- Pulpit: the word means "plundered." Philippi is the only church we know supported him; "wages" literally means soldiers' rations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/11.htm
- Chrysostom: "robbed" means stripping them of everything, not stealing in secret. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220221.htm

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: the verb tense suggests a crisis of poverty, not a constant state. "Burden" literally means "benumb," a word linked to the electric ray that numbs by touch. The help probably came with Silas and Timothy (Acts 18:5). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/11.htm
- Guzik links this help to Philippians 4:14–18. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-11/

**v. 10**
- Pulpit: this is a solemn oath, and "stopped" means stopping the mouth. Pulpit dismisses a theory about a wall across the Corinthian isthmus. Paul was especially careful among the Greeks of Achaia. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/11.htm

**v. 11**
- Guzik: Paul's embarrassing them comes only from love. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-11/
- Precept Austin calls "God knows" a formula of solemn affirmation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-11-commentary

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: the opening his opponents wanted was one he blocked by not taking money. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/11-12.htm
- Pulpit: this is biting sarcasm. Quoting Theodoret, it says the opponents boasted openly while secretly taking money. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/11.htm
- Storms: the opponents were financial parasites who would never minister for free. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/2-corinthians-11:1-33

**v. 13**
- Guzik: here Paul drops the sarcasm. No one can make himself a true apostle; only God's call does that. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-11/
- Pulpit: Bengel says Paul finally "calls a spade a spade." A true apostle carries someone else's message; these men served only themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/11.htm

**v. 14**
- Pulpit: the allusion may be to Jesus' temptation, to Satan among the angels in Job, or to a Jewish legend about Jacob's wrestling. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/11.htm
- Pulpit Homiletics suggests the Jewish party claimed angelic appearances or revelations, and Paul says they were deluded. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/2_corinthians/11.htm
- Guzik warns against being taken in by image and outward appearance. He quotes Hughes: anyone who makes outrageous claims can gain an undiscerning following. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-11/

**v. 15**
- Pulpit: they will be judged by what they are, as shown by their works, not by how they appear. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/11.htm
- Storms, citing Barnett: their "righteousness" was probably based on the Law of Moses rather than Christ's death. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/2-corinthians-11:1-33

**vv. 16–17**
- Pulpit: Paul feels a deep reluctance to talk about his own work, and has twice turned aside from the task. It says boasting may be a painful necessity, but in itself it can't be "after the Lord"; there is nothing Christlike in it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/11.htm
- Guzik: "not according to the Lord" means his defence centres on himself, and Paul didn't like talking about himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-11/

**v. 18**
- Storms: Paul deliberately plays his opponents' part. If they boast by worldly standards of strength, so will he, while making clear it is foolishness. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/2-corinthians-11:1-33

**v. 19**
- Guzik: biting sarcasm. If they are wise enough to put up with so many fools, they can listen to Paul for a while. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-11/

**v. 20**
- Guzik: the "bondage" may mean the false apostles were legalists putting people under the Law. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-11/
- Elsewhere Guzik quotes Carson: a backhanded slap was probably more insulting, and this verse probably has that kind of "insult slap" in mind. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/
- Homer Kent: the slap may mean insulting language, though religious leaders did sometimes use violence. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-11-commentary
- Storms goes through the five verbs: enslaving (legalism, domineering), devouring (perhaps money), taking advantage, self-exalting, and striking (literal or figurative). https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/2-corinthians-11:1-33

**v. 21**
- Pulpit: the meaning is uncertain. It may be an ironic admission that if staying away from such violent conduct is weakness, then he has been weak. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/11.htm
- Storms paraphrases the sarcasm: how shameful of me not to treat you as "kindly" as they have! https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/2-corinthians-11:1-33

**v. 22**
- Pulpit Homiletics: there were bitter suspicions that Paul was disloyal to his nation, so he was anxious to show he valued his ancestry and loved his people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/2_corinthians/11.htm

**v. 23**
- Pulpit points out the change in wording. Earlier Paul spoke "as a fool" (*aphron*); now it is the stronger *paraphron*, "out of my mind". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_corinthians/11.htm
- Chrysostom: against false apostles, Paul makes the comparison by pointing to the dangers he endured. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23101.htm
- Storms: Acts records only one imprisonment before this letter (Philippi), so Acts is only a partial history. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/2-corinthians-11:1-33

**v. 24**
- Storms: the 39 lashes come from Deuteronomy 25, given with a three-strapped whip (13 blows to the chest, 26 to the back). These floggings are mentioned nowhere else. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/2-corinthians-11:1-33

**v. 25**
- Storms: beatings with rods (Acts 16:22–23), though as a Roman citizen Paul should have been exempt; stoning (Acts 14:19). The three shipwrecks came before the one in Acts 27, so there were at least four. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/2-corinthians-11:1-33

**vv. 26–27**
- Storms links the dangers from countrymen and Gentiles to passages in Acts, and identifies the "false brothers" as Judaizers. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/2-corinthians-11:1-33
- Chrysostom: Paul scorned self-indulgence and found his comfort in hunger, beatings and prisons. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210213.htm

**vv. 28–29**
- Storms: his concern for the churches is the climax of the list, perhaps the worst trial of all. Paul felt his sheep's pain personally, as a true pastor. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/2-corinthians-11:1-33
- Guzik: Paul boasts only of weaknesses, including the daily burden for all the churches, the opposite of what the false apostles would claim. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-11/

**v. 30**
- Precept Austin: Paul shows that boasting isn't proper for a minister, turning the tables by boasting in weakness. Barton: his authority rested on God's appointment, not his abilities, and he could only show it by pointing to how God worked through his weakness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-11-commentary

**v. 31**
- I found no comment specific to this verse.

**vv. 32–33**
- Guzik: being let down in a basket was a picture of utter weakness, and it set the tone for Paul's whole apostolic life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-11/
- Chrysostom: Paul would not have mentioned the Damascus escape if circumstances had not required it. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23101.htm
- He also notes that Acts tells the story modestly, without making Paul seem important. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210120.htm
- Storms points to Acts 9:23. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/2-corinthians-11:1-33

---

**Modern triumphalist teaching:** The nearest these sources come is applying the chapter to "triumphalism":
- Guzik's "super Jesus" who never suffers (vv. 3–4): https://enduringword.com/putting-up-with-a-different-gospel/
- BibleHub says the critics promoted a triumphalist Christianity tied to eloquence, social status and money. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_compare_to_super-apostles_in_2_Cor.htm

None of these name prosperity or word-of-faith teaching, so I haven't claimed they do.
